It’s a place of surprising contrasts, featuring tranquil waterholes and deep river gorges. The crystal-clear waters that run through the park are a welcome sight on a hot summer’s day. Enjoy a picnic, a short walk, go for a refreshing swim, or take time out for quiet contemplation. Walks within the national park will take you through a diversity of vegetation and terrain, including picturesque Apsley Gorge. Experience marshlands, wet gullies and pockets of rainforest. Douglas-Apsley National Park may fly under the radar, but it protects an important swathe of dry eucalypt forest as well as numerous rare and endangered plants and animals. Get your parks pass Page Content ​​Nestled about halfway up Tasmania’s east coast, Douglas-Apsley National Park is full of delightful surprises and unexpected contrasts. Whether you’re looking for a gentle stroll and space for contemplation, a refreshing swim in a tranquil pool, or a challenging multi-day walk, this picturesque park has plenty to offer. Situated between the Douglas and Apsley rivers, the area has a long history of farming, mining and trapping, and contains one of the last remaining areas of uncleared dry forest in the state. The rivers which cut through the park have formed deep gorges and have created a number of beautiful pools. On a warm summer’s day, the turquoise waters of Apsley Waterhole are a favourite with families. Just a ten-minute walk from the car park at the south end of the park, it’s a great spot to cool off and relax before enjoying a picnic. Keep an eye out for wallabies in the area, but don’t be tempted to share your sandwiches. Walkers keen to explore the park more deeply and experience some of its diverse landscapes should consider the Apsley River Waterhole and Gorge Walk , which takes around 3-4 hours return. Starting on a forest track lined by eucalypts, you then descend a path of stacked boulders down to the stunning surroundings of the gorge. You can return the same way, or return by rock hopping downstream along the river bed. From the north of the park, experienced hikers can undertake the two-and-a-half-day Leeaberra Track walk. This is a challenging walk which rewards visitors with extensive views and spectacular landscapes. Bush camping is available at a number of sites within the park. See our page on Douglas-Apsley - campgrounds ​ for more information.​ Nature and conservation Show more/less ​​Overlooked by a dolerite-capped plateau, the forests and heathlands are home to an astonishing diversity of plants. In addition to a beautiful array of seasonal wildflowers and native orchids, the forests include 14 different tree species. Tasmanian blue gum, white peppermint and brown-topped stringybark are among the more common species, while Tasmanian ironbark and Barbers gum are considerably rarer. The park is a popular destination for birdwatchers and has been identified by BirdLife International as an Important Bird Area. It supports 11 of Tasmania’s 12 endemic bird species, as well as unique species such as the wedge-tailed eagle, spotted quail-thrush, and painted button-quail. The endangered swift parrot passes through during migration from Tasmania to mainland Australia, making this a perfect place to bring your binoculars. ​​In addition to the many rare plants and animals that can be found in the park, the Douglas and Apsley rivers are home to the Australian grayling: an endangered native fish which grows to about 30 cm. They are dark greenish to greyish olive along the back, lighter and silvery on the sides with a whitish belly. For more information on our wildlife please see Tasmania's wildlife . Visit our caring for wildlife page for more information on interacting with and protecting our native animals. Cultural heritage Show more/less Occupying the area of Douglas Apsley National Park is thought to be two bands within the northern end of the Oyster Bay nation. The Leetermairemener clans in the north between St Patricks Head and the Douglas River, and Plangermairemeener from the Douglas River south to the Swan River mouth. Each clan comprising of a number of family groups, between 30 to 80 people. Although clans were based in their own territory, they also moved over the territories of other friendly bands. It is possible that a route of traverse from the coast to the midlands may have existed during times of friendly relations. The most likely route was up the Douglas River to the Thompsons Marshes and then down the Dukes River to the midlands. The Leeaberra Track – named after the Aboriginal word for the Douglas River – is a reminder of the park’s rich pre-settlement and pre-industrial history. ​Douglas-Apsley is one of Tasmania’s newer national parks. Prior to the campaign that led to its protected status being declared in 1989 it had a long history of coal mining. The rugged landscape was criss-crossed with mining tracks, and coal was extracted from the area for over 100 years, from the mid-1800s onwards. Farmers and trappers also used the land for much of this time, whereas loggers only had very limited access. This pattern of land use, which favoured dry eucalypt forest, is why the area now contains one of the few largely un​cleared dry forests in Tasmania. Getting there Show more/less Buy a map from TasMap ​​​​​​​​​​Douglas-Apsley National Park is mid-way up the east coast of Tasmania, about 2¼ hours from Launceston and slightly longer from Hobart. The Apsley Waterhole, at the southern end of the park, is reached by taking the Rosedale Road off the A3 Tasman Highway about 3km north of Bicheno. Thompsons Marshes, at the northern end of the park, can only be reached on foot or via high clearance 4WD using the Forestry ‘E’ Road 24km north of Bicheno.​​​​​ Where possible, please avoid driving in our reserves at night. You are sharing the roads with our native wildlife, so take it slow and watch out for animals on the road. Know before you go Show more/less ​​​​​The southern end of the park has a carpark, toilets and a sign-posted walk to the Apsley Waterhole and lookout. ​ Other than a rough carpark, there are no facilities at the northern end of the park. The Park is a F​uel Stove Only ​area between October 1 and April 30. ​Please only use the established fire pits at the Apsley Waterhole campground. Water can be obtained from the Apsley River but please boil before use. The Douglas and Apsley Rivers are both subject to flooding following high rainfall and there are no bridges. When the rivers are flooded, do not attempt to cross them. The best alternative is to camp and wait for the rivers to subside. Otherwise simply turn back. It is wise to carry extra food in case of such days. ​ More information ​Find out other essential information for visiting Tasmania's parks and reserves on our Know Before You Go web page .
